newsitem.title: USA: Wall St grills Peru econ team on political outlook.
newsitem.headline: Wall St grills Peru econ team on political outlook.

text.p: Peru's economic team, which traveled to New York Wednesday to drum up investment, found itself pressed not about economic growth or fiscal policy, but about the country's political landscape.

U.S. financial analysts attending the roadshow made clear that, while Peru's economy was thriving, they were concerned about political turmoil such as the recent imbroglio over a key constitutional tribunal.

"The institutional and political questions weigh more heavily on my mind than the economic issues," said Joyce Chang, head of emerging market debt at Merrill Lynch, who spoke at a panel on Peru's future.
As soon as the conference was opened for questions, attendees pressed the panelists on recent political events in Peru. Policymakers played down the concerns.

"One cannot say that all the economic, democratic and social institutions are in place, but we're building on these institutions," said Beatriz Boza, president of the government's public relations unit Promperu.

In May, the head of Peru's highest constitutional court resigned to protest Congress' dismissal of three court members who had cast doubt on a law that would allow President Alberto Fujimori to run for a third term in 2000.
"What happened can be considered normal," Finance Minister Jorge Camet told Reuters. Camet said that the judges' dismissal was part of a legitimate legislative action typical in a democratic nation.
U.S. analysts cited a lack of political institutions and an overcentralization of power in President Fujimori as factors that could constrain the country's long-term potential.
Fujimori's popularity has plummeted in recent weeks to a 30 percent approval rating amid strong criticism of his administration's perceived authoritarianism.
"Politics is clearly their sore point," said one U.S. investor who attended the roadshow. "These guys are painfully aware that they don't have a pretty story on the politics."

Camet firmly stated that any political uncertainty would not affect the economy, which grew at 6.5 percent in May and a heady 7.2 percent over the first five months of 1997. U.S. analysts concurred that the economic returns look strong.
